The problem

A dashboard tells you what. Nobody has time to ask why.

MoveInSync moves 1M+ employees a day for 400+ organisations. The data streams 24/7 across timeliness, safety, cost, vendor performance and carbon. The bottleneck was never the data — it is the human who has to notice something, work out the cause, and decide what to do about it.

608,285Trips
1,636,453Commute records
716,336Attendance rows
51,699Safety incidents
What exists today

Charts, and a person

Every number is relative only to itself. Was ₹114/km good? Is 87% SLA acceptable? The dashboard cannot say. Someone has to know.

What breaks at scale

Signal buried in volume

608k trips a quarter produce far more anomalies than any transport manager can read. Alerting everything is the same as alerting nothing.

What we built

An agent that closes the loop

It notices, explains with evidence, decides who needs to know, drafts the action — and pauses for a human only where the stakes require it.

The requirement was to serve one persona. Serving all three only pays off if they are actually connected, so an unacknowledged alert escalates up the hierarchy on its own.

Nothing gets dropped by being ignored. An open, unacknowledged notification past its severity timeout — critical 1h, high 4h — is re-issued to the persona above, titled [Escalated] …, always immediate. info never escalates.
Personas & escalation03
Agentic designThe one-slide version

Sense → Gate → Reason → Act

The gate is the part that isn't in the brief. It sits before the LLM, not after, and decides whether a signal is worth thinking about at all.

Sense

9 detectors, parallel, pure SQL + thresholds. Zero LLM.

Gate

7 ordered rules → suppress / rule-only / escalate. Zero LLM.

Reason

SQL agent, benchmark lookup, deterministic impact context, then root cause.

Act

Notification, HTML report or drafted comms — with an interrupt() for sign-off.

Architecture in one slide04
Business impactUse case 1 · Transport Manager · safety

The hotspot nobody was looking for

Late-night trips where a female employee travelled without the mandated escort. It is a contract SLA term, it is a safety exposure, and before this it was buried in 608k trip rows.

Live capture — 90 days of real trip data. Colour is violation density; the agent’s own recommended actions sit under the strip.

The rule — detect_escort_compliance_signal
  • Window 21:00 → 06:00, LOGIN and LOGOUT legs
  • employee.gender = 'FEMALE' and trip.actual_escort = FALSE
  • Plus any open panic event — PANIC_MOBILE, WOMAN_TRAVELLING_ALONE
  • critical if the trip also ran ≥15 min late, otherwise high
5,525 unescorted late-night female trips surfaced in the demo window, and the org-wide compliance percentage is computed over the unbounded set — the 50-signal cap limits what gets dispatched, never what gets measured.
What the agent does with it

This signal type is pinned to safety_floor — it can never be suppressed, batched or tuned away — and is routed to communication, which drafts a warning notice to the vendor’s dispatch desk and stops for human approval.

Business impactUse case 2 · Line Manager · fairness

The same lateness, two opposite conclusions

One detector splits a late arrival into a transport failure or an attendance problem — because telling those apart is the entire job, and getting it wrong penalises the wrong person.

detect_attendance_correlation
  • ratio ≥ 0.60 → attendance_correlated_with_transport
    defend the employee, escalate the delay pattern
  • ratio ≤ 0.15 → attendance_unrelated_late
    this one is worth a direct conversation
  • Minimum 3 late samples; 25 signals per direction, worst first
The UI names the escalation target out loud: “escalate the underlying delay pattern to the Transport Manager rather than counting it against employees.”
67%Transport-caused → defend
14%Mixed
0%Employee-caused → talk

Team-wide split: only 17% of no-shows are shuttle-caused.

Per-employee verdict, in plain language, with the number that produced it.

Use case 2 · attendance correlation06
Business impactUse case 3 · Transport Head · money

Money on the table, named and quantified

Vendors bill by distance slab. The agent does not trust a rate card — it derives what each slab actually means from the org’s own billing history, then finds who is outside it.

detect_billing_discrepancy_signal
  • Slab bands from percentile_cont(0.5) per slab_name, min 20 samples, boundaries at adjacent-median midpoints
  • Expected cost per slab needs ≥5 samples before it is used
  • Vendor flagged at ≥3 trips and ≥₹500 exposure
  • Severity by share of that vendor’s spend — ≥20% critical, ≥12% high
₹13.1 lakhSlab leakage · May–Jul · all vendors
₹3.69 lakhLargest single vendor
15-day audit cycle → under five minutes, and it runs every scheduler tick rather than once a cycle. The vendor scorecard turns that into a contract conversation.

Live capture. Sneha leads on the headline SLA and is marginally cheaper per km — and logs 72% more safety incidents over the same window. That tension is the renewal argument, and it only appears once incidents are attributed to the vendor who actually ran each trip.

Use case 3 · billing audit07
Business impactMandatory · every metric carries context

Context is computed, not narrated

The brief asks that no metric arrives bare. We satisfy that in a node that never calls a model — so the context is always present, always consistent, and costs nothing.

# reason/state.py — attached to every decision
class ImpactContext(TypedDict):
    trend_direction:     str   # up | down | flat | unknown
    severity_band:       str   # low | medium | high | critical
    business_impact:     str   # one human sentence
    comparison_baseline: dict  # what, and how, it was compared
impact_context_builder is deliberately not an LLM call. Bands are arithmetic: flat inside ±2%, then 15% / 40% / 75% of magnitude. A model can be unavailable, over budget or wrong — the context on a card can’t be.
Not this

Emissions: 111 gCO₂/pkm

This

“Route 33 has averaged 111.2 gCO₂ per passenger-km since July 24 — 36% above the 82 gCO₂ ICE baseline.”

Live capture. Every card on every persona carries its own context_note — the comparison, the direction and the business consequence, generated for the card, not typed by us.

109,280 data-quality problems, logged and contained

The real dataset is not clean. A tenth detector exists purely to find that — and, crucially, it reports to nobody.

public.data_quality_flags — live counts
Issue typeCountWhere it comes from
null_required_field50,775Drivers without a licence number; completed trips with no arrival time
other31,385Alert severities carrying the literal string "False", plus 16,348 nulls
malformed_timestamp8,703Arrival more than a day from its own trip date

flag_data_quality routes to no persona. It is the only detector whose persona tuple is empty — every finding is written and auditable, and not one of them ever becomes a human’s inbox item. Data hygiene is an engineering backlog, not an operational alert.
Fixed on the way in
  • Comma-formatted trip_id strings coerced to int64
  • Placeholder stwid = 0 employee rows filtered out
  • Negative planned_km / traveled_km clipped to 0 and flagged
  • Mixed epoch/ISO timestamps harmonised
Found live, in the data

Some business units carry every late arrival on mode='cab' with zero 'shuttle' rows. A bare mode='shuttle' filter silently zeroed the correlation for those orgs. The fix — and the reason for it — is a comment in the detector SQL the trace shows the judge.

Architecture & code qualityDeployment view

System architecture

Seven containers. Two ways in — a 5-minute scheduler tick and a Postgres LISTEN/NOTIFY event — and one way back out to the browser.

System architecture10
Architecture & code qualityCan it scale?

No node in this codebase knows a table name

Every entity and column a detector, chart or metric touches is resolved through one mapping file. That is the whole answer to “would this survive contact with your production schema?”

# backend/config/data_contract.yaml — 397 lines, version 2
entities:
  trip:
    table: mis.trip
    columns:
      scheduled_time:  scheduled_arrival
      actual_time:     actual_arrival
      actual_escort:   actual_escort
      traveled_km:     traveled_km
# and in every node, without exception:
contract = get_contract().entity("trip")
table, c = contract.table, contract.column
SELECT {c('actual_time')} FROM {table} …
Repointing the whole system at MoveInSync’s real schema is one file and zero code changes — set DATA_CONTRACT_PATH at a different mapping and every detector, chart and report follows. 17 of 17 entities validate on boot.
What that buys, concretely
  • The SQL agent’s table allow-list is derived from the contract — checkpoint, store and pipeline tables are invisible to the model by construction
  • Column renames in the warehouse never reach application code
  • The same agent runs on a synthetic schema and the real mis.* one
17/17Entities valid
0Hardcoded tables
1File to repoint
Data contract11
Agentic designThe centrepiece

LangGraph agentic architecture

Four compiled StateGraphs. Act is embedded in the top graph as a real subgraph node, so interrupt() and Command(resume=…) persist on the parent thread.

LangGraph architecture12
Agentic designTyped state at every boundary

Graph state — the contract between nodes

Nothing is passed as a loose dict. Each subgraph declares what it consumes and what it is allowed to add, and the reducer on signals is what makes nine parallel detectors safe.

SenseState — fan-out producer 
org_id: str
since: datetime | None
event: dict | None
signals: Annotated[list[Signal], operator.add]
dq_issues_found: int

# the reducer above is the whole reason nine
# detector nodes can write concurrently

        severity · summary · raw_metric · source
ReasonState — routing + evidence 
gate_mode · gate_reason · gate_confidence
route: "sql" | "research" | "both" | "context_only"
sql_result:      SQLAgentResult | None
research_result: ResearchComparison | None
impact_context:  ImpactContext | None
decision:        ReasonDecision | None

ReasonDecision: summary · root_cause · recommendation
   confidence · needs_human_signoff · target_persona
   supporting_evidence

question · org_id · table_names · schema_context
generated_sql: str
sql_retry_count: int          # hard cap 3
query_error_log: list[str]    # fed back to the model
result_rows · final_answer · success · done
out_of_scope · out_of_scope_reason

Agentic designRules & thresholds

Nine detectors, and every number in them is configurable

DetectorFires whenEscalates to criticalGoes to
delay_breach≥25% of route trips breach 15 min, or avg delay ≥20 min (≥3 trips)avg ≥35 min or ≥80% breachedTransport Mgr
incidentUnresolved and severity ≥ mediumseverity = criticalTransport Mgr
escort_compliance_violationUnescorted female trip, 21:00–06:00, or open panic eventtrip also ≥15 min lateTransport Mgr
performance_variabilityCoefficient of variation ≥ 20% over ≥15 samples, 10-min floorCV ≥ 2× threshold → highTransport Mgr
cost_divergence≥20% off contract rate or fleet average (≥3 trips)≥50% divergenceTransport Mgr + Head
billing_discrepancy≥3 flagged trips and ≥₹500, slab bands from ≥20 samples≥20% of vendor spendTransport Head
emissions_over_target≥1.05× the 82 gCO₂/passenger-km baseline≥1.5× baselineTransport Head
attendance_correlatedTransport-correlation ratio ≥ 0.60 (≥3 lates)ratio ≥0.85 → highLine Manager
attendance_unrelated_lateCorrelation ratio ≤ 0.15—Line Manager
flag_data_qualityNulls, duplicates, malformed timestamps, out-of-range values—nobody, by design
None of these are constants in code. Each is a default that an alert_rules row overrides per organisation and per signal type — JSON params, gate mode and notification cadence — cached for 30 seconds and editable from the Settings page, live within one scheduler tick. A 7-day lookback anchors on the last date with real volume, not wall-clock.
Rules & thresholds14
Agentic design & cost at scaleThe filtering gate

Seven rules decide whether an LLM is worth it

First match wins. Every decision — including every suppression — is written to gate_decisions and shows up in the trace.

#RuleActionConf.
1safety_floorescalate incidents, escort violations, anything critical — not overridable1.00
2operator_overrideforced an operator’s explicit Settings choice1.00
3suppression_heartbeatescalate 5 consecutive suppressions — nothing hides forever0.90
4insufficient_samplesuppress below the detector’s minimum sample size0.70
5recurrencesuppress already dispatched 3× in 24h0.60
6high_margin_breachrule-only ≥2× over threshold and proven FP rate ≤20%0.50–0.95
7default_escalateescalate when nothing else matched0.50
The safeguards are the interesting part. A scope can never be suppressed indefinitely — rule 3 has already fired 16 times on this data, forcing suppressed scopes back into view. And rule_only demands a proven low false-positive rate: a signal type with no dispatch history yet always escalates. Unknown is never treated as safe.
The filtering gate15
Agentic design & cost at scaleWhere the model actually runs

Five LLM call sites in the entire system

Everything that can be arithmetic is arithmetic. The model is spent on the two things it is genuinely better at: writing SQL, and explaining a cause in a sentence a human will act on.

Calls the model · 5 sites
generate_queryText-to-SQL, grounded on live DDL + 3 sample rows · 8192 tok
synthesize_answerAnswers strictly from returned rows · 2048 tok
root_cause_synthesizerSignal + context + SQL evidence → cause & recommendation · 1024 tok
communication_drafterAudience-tuned notice, under 120 words · 12288 tok
report narrativeLeadership summary over a period · 12288 tok

Structured output is prompt-and-parse (fenced JSON → regex → json.loads), never tool-calling — a deliberate choice for a non-frontier model.

Never calls the model
  • all 9 detectors
  • poll_or_event_entry
  • evaluate_gate
  • route_to_specialist
  • impact_context_builder
  • rule_based_decision
  • smalltalk_reply
  • bridge_to_act
  • check_query (the guard)
  • every act router
Routing is a keyword check, not a model call. Asking a model which specialist to use would double the cost of every turn to answer a question a frozenset already answers.
Model

sarvam-105b-conversations over an OpenAI-compatible endpoint. Provider and model are environment variables — LLM_PROVIDER / LLM_MODEL — not an import.

LLM call map16
Agentic design & cost at scaleProven under load

The budget guard, caught doing its job

A circuit breaker only counts if it has actually tripped. Ours did — in this instance, today — and the system degraded instead of falling over.

# llm/provider.py — a subclass, not a wrapper
class _BudgetGuardedChatOpenAI(ChatOpenAI):
    # overrides _generate / _agenerate / _stream / _astream
    # so bind_tools() and with_structured_output()
    # physically cannot route around the check

    INCR llm_calls:{provider}:{date}   # TTL 26h
    if count > daily_limit:
        raise LLMBudgetExhaustedError   # before the HTTP call
The counter increments before the request leaves the process, so a crash mid-call cannot under-count. Over budget, the API returns 503 — never a fabricated 200.
What actually happened here

The scheduler hit the 500-call ceiling. 90 escort-compliance signals were refused at root_cause_synthesizer with LLMBudgetExhaustedError — and each one was logged as “will retry automatically next cycle,” not lost, not half-written, not crashed.

Live capture. Budget, suppression and false-positive rate per signal type are operator-facing — and the copy is explicit that safety hotspots “cannot be tuned away”.

Cost at scale17
Architecture & code qualityThe SQL agent · no-write rule

A model writes the query. It is not trusted to.

Text-to-SQL over a production warehouse is the highest-risk thing in this system, so the guarantee is structural rather than instructional.

The hard boundary — security.py
  • Parsed with sqlglot into an AST, never regex
  • Rejects more than one statement — no ; stacking
  • Rejects anything that is not exp.Select
  • Walks the whole tree rejecting Insert · Update · Delete · Drop · Alter · Create · Truncate · Grant · Command
Blast radius
  • LIMIT 200 injected if absent, lowered if higher, re-capped after execution
  • statement_timeout = 8000ms set on the connection itself
  • Table allow-list derived from the data contract — checkpoint and internal tables are invisible
  • org_id filter required by prompt and schema context
Failing honestly
  • 3 retries, each fed the previous SQL and every error, then fail_closed — it never guesses
  • A truncated generation counts as a retry rather than being parsed as SQL
  • Out-of-scope questions hit decline — no SQL is ever executed
Prompt injection is treated as expected input, not an edge case: the question is passed as data, and the guard — not the instruction — is what makes a write impossible. A jailbroken model still cannot reach a mutating statement.
SQL agent guardrails18
FunctionalityConversational copilot

Ask it anything the warehouse can answer

The same graph, entered without a signal. POST /api/chat runs reason with skip_act=True, so a question never dispatches a notification.

Live capture — answered from 1.6M commute rows, with a trace link on every message.

One identifier, three jobs

chat_threads.id is the LangGraph checkpoint thread_id is the episodic-memory user_id. Memory is namespaced ("memories", persona, thread_id, "episodic"), so forgetting a conversation is exact — one thread, nothing else.

Honest failure
  • Budget exhausted or provider unconfigured → 503
  • Anything else → 502
  • Never a 200 carrying an invented answer
Small talk is short-circuited by a keyword check before any node runs — greeting the agent costs a database round trip of exactly zero and an LLM call of exactly zero.
Conversational agent19
FunctionalityTransparency · audit trail

Every claim on screen can be opened

“How was this computed?” is on every card and every chat message. It replays the agent’s own checkpoint history — no separate instrumentation was added to produce it.

Live capture — the generated SQL, the rows it returned, and the confidence behind the recommendation.

The seven step kinds
  • Signal Detected — carries the detector’s own SQL, stashed in raw_metric
  • Gate Evaluated — action, reason, matched rule, confidence
  • SQL Generated — the query, and the retry count
  • SQL Executed — rows returned, self-corrections, last error
  • Impact Context Attached — the business-impact sentence
  • Decision — cause, confidence, and a separate recommended action
  • Escalated — recurses into the original thread’s history
build_trace() is a formatter. It reads get_state_history() off the checkpointer and reaches outside it exactly once — for the gate row, which is written before the graph is invoked. Transparency is a property of the architecture, not a feature bolted onto it.
Trace & transparency20
FunctionalityAutonomy with a brake

It acts on its own — except where it shouldn’t

Autonomy is the point, but a warning notice to a vendor’s dispatch desk is not something a model should send unsupervised. So the graph stops.

# act/nodes.py — a real LangGraph pause, not a flag
approval = interrupt({
    "type": "approval_request",
    "draft": communication_draft, …
})
# the graph halts here; state is checkpointed to Postgres.
# resumed later, from anywhere, on the same thread_id:
graph.invoke(Command(resume={"approved": True,
                             "approver": user}), config)
Re-clicking Approve cannot double-send. Idempotency comes from the thread’s checkpoint, not from a status column we remember to check — the node replays from the top and the interrupt() resolves once.
Who gets stopped
  • Incidents and escort violations — routed to communication, always sign-off
  • Everything else dispatches autonomously as a notification
  • The scheduler generates daily, weekly and monthly reports on its own cadence

Live capture — the agent’s own activity log. Every entry here was produced by a scheduler tick or a database event, with nobody at the keyboard.
